{
    "id": "02-reasoning/pareto-analysis",
    "title": "Pareto Analysis",
    "category": "02-reasoning",
    "level": "basic",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Rank causes or contributors by their share of an effect, find the few inputs that produce most of the outcome, and act on that measured concentration.",
    "body": "Pareto Analysis Category: Reasoning | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Most effects are concentrated: a minority of causes produces the majority of results. Pareto analysis measures that concentration instead of assuming it — ranking contributors by measured share, identifying the set that crosses a stated threshold, and directing effort where leverage is real. The skill is about the measurement, not the folklore: not every distribution is 80/20, and the split must be computed, not quoted. When to Use Use when effort must be allocated across many candidate causes — defect sources, error classes, cost drivers, usage patterns — and the budget cannot cover everything. Do not cite the 80/20 ratio as a finding; measure the actual concentration and report the real split. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Measured contribution per cause | | | | No | Cumulative share defining the vital few; default 0.8 | | | | No | Display names per cause | Procedure 1. Measure contributions on a single, stated scale; shares computed across mixed units are meaningless. 2. Sort causes by contribution, descending, and compute each one as a share of the total. 3. Accumulate shares in rank order and identify the smallest set that crosses the threshold. 4. Report the actual split — how many causes reach what cumulative share — instead of the assumed 80/20. 5. Check the tail: the long tail still matters when it aggregates, and concentration at the top does not make the rest zero. 6. Re-measure after acting on the vital few; the distribution shifts once the top contributors are addressed. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Causes in descending contribution order | | | | Smallest set crossing the cumulative threshold | | | | Actual cause-count to cumulative-share split measured | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Assumed split | The 80/20 ratio is quoted rather than measured | Compute and report the actual split | | Mixed scales | Shares computed across incommensurable units | Measure on one stated scale | | Static ranking | An old distribution guides new effort | Re-measure after each intervention | | Tail neglect | The aggregated tail is dismissed as zero | Report tail totals alongside the vital few | | Single-cause rounding | Near-equal causes split arbitrarily | Note ranks that are statistically indistinguishable | Security and Authority Boundary Pareto rankings over incident, access, or failure data can reveal which components of a system are most fragile. Treat the ranking itself as sensitive when the underlying data is, and share it on a need-to-know basis. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia's overview of the Pareto principle (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paretoprinciple). 2.     "description": "Sample N independent reasoning chains for the same question and majority-vote the final answer. Trades cost for accuracy — robust on math and logic, surprisingly cheap with smaller-than-frontier models.",
    "body": "Self-Consistency Description Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022) augments Chain of Thought by sampling N independent reasoning chains at temperature > 0, parsing each one's final answer, and majority-voting. Wrong reasoning chains tend to scatter across many wrong answers; correct reasoning converges. So the modal answer is usually the right one.     "body": "Sensitivity Analysis Category: Reasoning | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Any computed recommendation rests on inputs with different leverage. Sensitivity analysis varies each input across a stated range, observes the output response, and ranks which inputs actually drive the conclusion — turning a raw model output into a statement of the form: the conclusion holds unless a named assumption moves by more than a stated amount. When to Use Use before committing to a decision, forecast, or model-based recommendation when inputs are uncertain and someone needs to know which uncertainty matters. Vary one input at a time across its stated range with others held at nominal values, recording the output response. 3. Rank inputs by output swing and identify which ones cross decision thresholds. 4. Where inputs interact, sample combinations with a Monte Carlo design and report joint effects, not just single-input swings. 5. Report the ranges tested; a sensitivity claim outside the tested range is an extrapolation. 6. State t he consequence: which input, moved how far, reverses the conclusion.
